  "chapter_body_excerpt": "“Danxi said…” The textual life of medical ideas on madness, 1360-1530 Danxi said that dian belongs to Yin and kuang to Yang, that dian is excessive joy and kuang excessive anger. He also stated that the doubling of Yin is dian and the doubling of Yang is kuang. 丹溪謂癲屬陰 狂屬陽 癲多喜 狂多怒 又云重陰者癲 重陽者狂 Xu Chunfu 徐春甫 in Gujin yitong daquan 古今醫統大全 (1556) $ ^{1} $ Chapters 3 and 4 traced a momentous transformation in the etiology of madness from Wind to internal Fire and mucus between the twelfth and the fourteenth century. The Ming dynasty (1368-1644) was not a period of strong epistemological breaks in medicine, but one in which physicians re-orchestrated earlier approaches to form new doctrinal and therapeutic emphases. Xu Chunfu above was citing the Danxi xinfa 丹溪心法, a composite work compiled and printed in his own Huizhou Prefecture (Anhui) in the early 1480s and that quickly became the most influential work attributed to Zhu Zhenheng 朱震亨 (\"Danxi\" 丹溪: 1282-1358). This and the next chapter show how the development of Ming medical thinking on dian and kuang was shaped by three important trends that are well symbolized by Xu's quotation: the rising influence of precepts attributed to Danxi, the importance of Huizhou as a center of medical theorizing and publication, and the profound intertextuality of the elite medical tradition. ### 5.1 Intertextual composition and the Danxi corpus The “Danxi corpus” in the history of medical thinking on madness The rise to prominence of a body of teachings attributed to Zhu Zhenheng deeply shaped Ming medical thinking and practice.
